questions.blueprintObjective: Apply occupied schedule knowledge while the electrician installs building automation systems.

questions.question: During commissioning of a replacement DDC controller for AHU-3, the operator graphics screen shows the duct smoke-detector alarm point annunciating under the wrong zone. What should the electrician do to confirm the alarm mapping is correct before commissioning continues?
options: Edit the zone name on the graphics page so the label matches the zone the detector actually annunciates in.
Restore the saved database file from the controller that was removed and let it overwrite the current point configuration.
Verify the alarm mapping against the approved points list, sequence of operation, and manufacturer configuration data.
Log the mismatch on the deficiency list and finish the remaining commissioning checks before returning to the alarm point.
questions.explanation: A smoke-detector point mapped to the wrong zone can send a life-safety signal to the wrong location, delaying response or masking a real hazard. The approved points list and sequence of operation define the intended addressing and shutdown logic, and the manufacturer configuration data confirms how the replacement controller's inputs were set up, so comparing all three against the actual input and output behaviour proves the mapping before the system is relied on. Renaming the graphic to match what is observed only hides the addressing error, because the underlying point still drives the wrong zone logic and interlocks. Restoring the old controller's database may carry forward the same faulty mapping and can overwrite correct settings made during the replacement. Deferring the check to a deficiency list leaves a life-safety point unverified while the rest of the system is being placed in service, so the mapping must be confirmed before commissioning moves on.
questions.sourceReference: MWA E, Task E-28, Sub-task E-28.02
questions.blueprintObjective: Apply alarm mapping knowledge while the electrician installs building control systems.

questions.question: After replacing a failed BACnet controller on air handler E28-06, the supervising electrician sees that several AI and AO point addresses on the new device do not match the original points list in the commissioning package. The technician suggests using the same mapping they remember from a similar air handler on another floor and putting the unit back into service. What must the supervising electrician require before the controller is energized and put under automatic control?
options: Accept the technician’s recollection from the other floor as adequate proof that the point mapping is correct for E28-06.
Energize the controller immediately and use the first automatic start-up as the primary test of point mapping.
Pause the restart, verify each point address against the approved drawings and sequences for E28-06, correct any mismatches, and document the final mapping changes.
Approve the point mapping because the replacement controller model and air handler cabinet appear identical to the earlier installation.
questions.explanation: When a replacement controller’s point addresses do not match the original commissioning documentation, the mapping for that specific air handler must be verified before the controller is energized. Using point mapping from another floor or a similar unit can route commands and feedback to the wrong sensors, actuators, or safety interlocks, leading to unstable operation or bypassed protection once the system starts. The supervising electrician needs the technician to stop the restart, compare each input and output address to the current drawings and written sequence for E28-06, correct any discrepancies, and record the final mapping so future technicians know exactly how the controller is configured. This ensures that airflow, temperature, and safety points respond as intended when the system is powered and placed in automatic service.

questions.question: During commissioning of a hot water valve actuator serving a critical process heating loop, a simulated power-loss test shows the valve driving fully open instead of the specified fail-closed position, risking overheating. What is the most appropriate troubleshooting response?
options: Accept the vendor's fail-safe claim without testing because the same actuator model performed correctly on another site.
Bypass the fail-safe verification step to keep the loop online while assuming the actuator spring is fine.
Adjust several actuator and controller parameters together, then call any brief stabilization proof of correction.
Isolate the valve function, verify the fail-safe response, correct the confirmed cause, then repeat the controlled functional test.
questions.explanation: The observed evidence—an actuator driving open instead of the specified closed position during a simulated power-loss test—confirms a fail-safe fault that could overheat a critical process loop. Isolating the function, retesting against approved sequence documentation, correcting only the confirmed cause (such as spring return failure or wrong fail action configuration), and repeating the controlled test verifies the fix without introducing new risk. Accepting the vendor's claim ignores contrary test evidence from this specific installation. Bypassing verification to keep the loop online leaves an unconfirmed, unsafe fail-safe state in place. Changing multiple parameters simultaneously prevents isolating which change actually corrected the fault, and treating temporary stabilization as proof risks masking an intermittent or unresolved failure mode that could recur under real power-loss conditions.

questions.blueprintObjective: Apply fail-safe state knowledge while the electrician installs building automation systems.

questions.question: While reviewing trend logs for an air-handling unit after a firmware update, an electrician sees that the supply-air temperature trend no longer follows the commissioned setpoint profile and a prior alarm has no documented cause. How should the electrician proceed to restore reliable control of this AHU?
options: Change several PID loop tuning parameters at the same time and assume any short-term improvement confirms the problem is solved.
Copy the supply-air temperature trend from a similar air-handling unit in another building and use it as the new baseline without checking this unit’s sequence.
Stop adjustments, review the trend data against the approved sequence of operations and commissioning records, correct the identified cause of the mismatch, and record the action taken.
Replace the supply-air temperature sensor showing the greatest calibration drift and only record a cause if the alarm reappears later.
questions.explanation: When trend data deviates from the commissioned setpoint profile after a firmware change and the alarm cause is unknown, the priority is to verify how the system is supposed to operate before making further changes. Comparing the current trend to the approved sequence of operations and commissioning documentation helps the electrician identify whether the issue is due to control logic, configuration, or a true hardware fault. Once the source of the mismatch is found and corrected, documenting the action ensures future technicians can understand what was changed and why. Changing multiple tuning parameters at once makes it difficult to trace which adjustment caused the effect and can hide the real problem. Using a baseline from another unit ignores differences in equipment and control sequences, which can lead to improper operation. Replacing sensors without confirming that they are the cause may waste time and materials and can leave a control programming issue unresolved.

questions.question: An air handling unit has run in manual override for several months after a nuisance freezestat alarm. A tenant fit-up now requires the automatic sequence to resume. Before removing the override on unit E28-09, what should the electrician confirm first?
options: Return the unit to automatic and watch discharge air temperature through one full occupied cycle before checking anything else.
Confirm override status against the approved control drawings, equipment ratings, manufacturer data, and current field readings.
Match the occupied and unoccupied setpoints on the building automation graphic to the tenant's new schedule and save the change.
Have the building operator describe the original nuisance alarm and enter that description as the record of the override's cause.
questions.explanation: An extended override can mask a real fault, so returning to automatic control without verification risks unstable operation, incorrect commands, or loss of protective action such as freeze protection. Comparing the override status against approved control drawings, rated equipment parameters, manufacturer data, and measured field values confirms whether the original cause is resolved before automatic sequencing is restored. Releasing the unit to automatic and observing one cycle tests the system with an unverified fault still possible and no baseline to interpret what is seen. Adjusting occupied and unoccupied setpoints addresses the tenant schedule but does nothing to prove the overridden point, sensor, or interlock now functions as designed. An operator's spoken account of the alarm is useful background, but it is not measured evidence and cannot confirm current device condition or wiring integrity. Only the verified, documented comparison supports a traceable decision that the next shift can independently confirm.

questions.question: A rooftop AHU shows an intermittent heating/cooling staging fault: every third operating cycle, one stage is skipped, and the issue appears only on cool mornings when the system is first starting up. Occupants report short temperature swings. What is the most reliable way to resolve the problem?
options: Use the building operator's memory of normal operation as the acceptance record for the sequence.
Finish the remaining programming and make the next full start-up the first verification of the sequence.
Isolate the affected control loop, verify the sequence logic against the points list, correct the confirmed cause, then repeat a controlled functional test.
Accept the sequence as correct because a similar AHU worked properly on another project.
questions.explanation: An intermittent staging fault that appears in a specific operating window usually points to a real condition such as sensor drift, a timing conflict, or a point-mapping error. The most reliable response is to isolate the control loop, test the sequence under controlled conditions, correct the confirmed fault, and repeat the functional test to prove the sequence now works consistently. Memory, earlier success on another job, or waiting for an occupied start-up does not verify this specific unit's behavior.

questions.question: During commissioning of a rooftop unit’s discharge air loop, you are tracing the signal flow shown in the closed-loop diagram: the discharge air transmitter sends its scaled signal to the controller input, the controller drives the modulating valve actuator, the valve changes discharge temperature in the duct, and the resulting temperature is fed back to the controller through the same transmitter. The approved points list shows the discharge air transmitter and controller input are supposed to be scaled 0–100°C, but you discover the transmitter is programmed for 0–50°C while the controller input is still set for 0–100°C, and the valve is hunting around the setpoint. Because the feedback entering the controller from the sensor block is roughly twice the actual discharge temperature across the operating range, what should you do next to restore stable, accurate control?
options: Adjust only the controller tuning by widening the proportional band and increasing the integral time so the valve moves more slowly, leaving the discharge air transmitter scaled 0–50°C against the controller’s 0–100°C input range.

Keep the existing 0–50°C transmitter range and add a fixed correction factor at the controller input so the displayed discharge temperature matches a calibrated thermometer at the current operating condition.

Install a new discharge air transmitter with a nominal 0–100°C capability and recheck valve stroke, assuming the hunting is the result of a failing sensor element rather than a configuration mismatch.

Take the loop out of automatic while you work, reprogram the discharge air transmitter to the specified 0–100°C span, confirm in the diagrammed signal path that the controller input scaling now matches the transmitter output, then verify the feedback tracks an actual temperature reading and document the updated settings.
questions.explanation: In the closed-loop path shown, the controller’s decisions depend entirely on the scaled signal coming from the sensor measurement block at its input. If the discharge air transmitter is programmed for 0–50°C but the controller input is still scaled for a 0–100°C span, the controller interprets the feedback as roughly twice the real temperature over the operating range. This causes the controller to overdrive the modulating valve, the discharge air temperature to overshoot, and the loop to hunt as the mis-scaled feedback continuously reinforces the error. The proper corrective action is to remove the loop from automatic, reset the transmitter to the specified 0–100°C span, and then confirm at the controller input—in direct reference to the diagrammed measurement-to-controller block—that the scaling now matches the transmitter output. Once the input range and sensor span agree, the feedback follows the actual discharge temperature, allowing the loop to stabilize; documenting the new settings leaves a clear record for future service. Simply retuning proportional and integral terms leaves the measurement span wrong, so the loop may respond more slowly but still controls to an incorrect temperature. A fixed offset cannot repair a span error, because the error changes with the reading and only lines up at one trimmed point. Replacing the transmitter assumes a hardware failure when the device is working; with the wrong range programmed, a new unit would produce the same hunting until the scaling mismatch in the diagrammed sensor-to-controller path is corrected.

questions.question: An office zone served by air handler AHU-6 is overheating. At the controller the electrician observes: discharge-air temperature is stable at 18 °C, the chilled-water valve is nearly closed, and the active discharge-air cooling setpoint is 18 °C even though the intended occupied cooling target for this air handler is 13 °C. What is the most appropriate action to restore proper cooling control?
options: Adjust the discharge-air temperature sensor calibration so the controller reads about 5 °C colder than the actual air temperature, forcing the existing loop to drive the chilled-water valve further open.
Reduce the throttling range of the cooling control loop so that even a small difference between measured temperature and setpoint causes the chilled-water valve to move rapidly toward full open.

Determine what is commanding the 18 °C discharge-air setpoint — such as a supply-air reset strategy, an occupied/unoccupied or warm-up mode, or a high‑priority local override — correct the source so the setpoint returns to 13 °C, then verify the valve modulates to maintain that target.
Manually position the chilled-water valve to a fixed mid‑range opening during occupied hours so the coil delivers more cooling while leaving the discharge-air setpoint at 18 °C.
questions.explanation: The loop is operating as designed: the measured discharge-air temperature matches the active setpoint, so the controller is correctly driving the chilled-water valve nearly closed to hold 18 °C. The problem is that the setpoint in use does not match the required occupied cooling target of 13 °C. To correct the condition, the electrician must find and adjust the logic that writes the discharge-air setpoint, such as a supply-air reset function, a mode that is still enforcing a higher value, or an override at a higher command priority. Restoring the 13 °C setpoint and confirming that the valve then strokes open and the discharge temperature drops demonstrates that the control loop maintains the proper target. Changing sensor calibration to force a colder reading deliberately falsifies the feedback signal, which can corrupt alarms, trends, and reset strategies and makes later troubleshooting difficult. Narrowing the throttling range alters loop gain and can cause hunting and unstable temperatures, but it does not change the fact that the controller is satisfied with an incorrect setpoint. Fixing the valve at a constant mid‑open position bypasses automatic control, allowing discharge temperature to drift with load and flow, wasting energy and failing to address the root cause: the wrong discharge-air setpoint value.

questions.question: During an economizer functional test on a rooftop unit, a modulating outdoor air damper actuator drives fully closed whenever the BAS issues a 100% open command, and the space temperature keeps rising. Before returning this BAS point to automatic operation, what should the electrician verify on the actuator and its control circuit?
options: That the 24 V supply polarity, voltage level, and transformer loading at the actuator terminals are within the nameplate operating range under full stroke

That the actuator’s selected rotation direction and the way its control signal leads are landed cause the damper to open on an increasing BAS command, consistent with the documented sequence of operation
That the mixed air and outdoor air temperature sensors near the damper section read correctly when compared to a calibrated reference thermometer under stable airflow
That the BAS analog output range has been adjusted so the percentage command displayed at the operator workstation matches the current damper position trend
questions.explanation: The symptom—damper closing as the BAS commands it open—shows the actuator is responding smoothly but in the opposite direction to the control signal, not that it lacks power. A modulating actuator has a selectable rotation direction and specific signal-to-travel relationship, and these must match the sequence of operation so that higher open commands drive the damper toward the outdoor air position and the spring return fails the damper to the intended fail-safe state. Verifying the direction setting and how the control signal wiring is landed, then stroking the damper from 0% to 100% under supervision, confirms that the damper will open on an increasing command. Checking supply voltage and transformer loading is more relevant when an actuator stalls, chatters, or cannot complete a stroke, which is not the case when it moves freely but backwards. Sensor calibration affects when the economizer enables and how it modulates based on temperature or enthalpy, but it does not change the mechanical direction of actuator travel for a given signal. Adjusting the BAS output scaling so the display matches a reversed mechanical movement would only mask the underlying problem while leaving the spring-return and any hardwired overrides operating in the wrong direction during faults or manual operation.

questions.question: During business hours, a VAV zone controller E28-14 occasionally drops to its unoccupied setpoints for a few minutes and then returns to normal, but the trend logs show that this only happens when the nearby 30 kW supply fan drive transitions through certain speeds. The controller is programmed to fall back to unoccupied defaults whenever it stops receiving the global occupied schedule broadcast from the BAS front end over the communication trunk. What is the most reliable next step to confirm and address the root cause?
options: Adjust the unoccupied heating and cooling setpoints at the controller so the zone remains comfortable whenever the fallback occurs.
Extend the front end’s occupied schedule to cover more hours so the controller is less likely to be commanded to unoccupied during the day.

Trend the controller’s communication status while the drive ramps through the speeds that coincide with the issue to verify if the schedule broadcast is being disrupted, then correct any cable routing, shielding, or bonding problems and retest under the same operating conditions.
Replace the zone temperature sensor and damper actuator on the VAV box and ask occupants to report whether comfort complaints continue.
questions.explanation: The controller is programmed to revert to unoccupied defaults when it stops receiving the global occupied schedule, so intermittent drops only when the nearby drive changes speed point to communication interference rather than a local hardware fault. By trending the controller’s communication status while the drive ramps, you can confirm whether the broadcast is being disrupted at specific speeds, then correct issues such as poor cable separation from power conductors, improper shield termination, or inadequate bonding and verify the fix by repeating the same operating condition. Adjusting unoccupied setpoints masks the symptom but leaves the communication problem uncorrected, so control remains unreliable. Extending the occupied schedule changes how often the controller is commanded occupied but does not eliminate the trunk disturbance that can also affect other devices. Replacing the zone temperature sensor and damper actuator addresses components that follow whatever setpoints the controller applies; they do not cause the controller to lose the schedule broadcast or change modes on their own.

questions.question: On a rooftop air-handling unit, a supply-air high-temperature safety switch is physically wired into controller input 4. In the controller database, input 4 is currently mapped to the software point "Exhaust Fan Status," but the approved points list shows input 4 assigned to "Supply Air High Temp." When the switch closes, the workstation shows an exhaust fan status change and no high-temperature alarm. What should the electrician do to correct this mismatch between the field device, the controller input, and the software point name?
options: Change only the text label on the workstation graphic so the event appears as a supply-air high-temperature condition, without altering the controller point mapping for input 4.
Move the high-temperature switch conductors onto a different input that is already mapped as exhaust fan status so the field wiring matches the current database configuration.
Create a new software point for supply-air high temperature, leave input 4 mapped to exhaust fan status, and use both points to report the same contact closure.

Re-address controller input 4 in the database to the "Supply Air High Temp" point defined on the approved points list, then trip the switch to verify the correct alarm appears at the workstation and update the documentation accordingly.
questions.explanation: The supply-air high-temperature switch, the controller input, and the software point name must all represent the same function for the alarm to operate as intended. The correct action is to remap controller input 4 to the "Supply Air High Temp" point specified on the approved points list, then operate the switch to confirm that the proper high-temperature alarm and associated logic appear at the workstation, and finally record the change in the system documentation. Simply relabelling the workstation graphic leaves the controller logic tied to the wrong point, so interlocks, trends, and priorities continue to behave as if the signal were exhaust fan status. Moving the wiring to a different input to match the existing database ignores the approved points list and leaves input 4 with no meaningful monitoring. Creating an extra software point from the same contact causes duplicate events from one device and still does not resolve the conflict between the programmed mapping and the design intent.
